title: Retention vs acquisition: ceiling, replacement and penetration
origin: ClimbOS synthesis (original proposal) from the member frameworks; author guidance is cited by finding id, proposed rules are labelled 'proposed'.
decision_task: How much effort goes to keeping customers vs winning new buyers, using the steady-state ceiling and replacement arithmetic.
applies_when: Owner asks whether to focus on retention or acquisition
Growth goal relies on buying frequency alone
evidence_requirements: churn reasons split: controllable (value, onboarding, service) vs uncontrollable (moved, closed, no longer needs, budget)
category or size-matched churn norm if any
customers (or accounts) who bought in the last 12 months
purchases or visits per buyer in that period
rough count of category buyers in the reachable area (estimate allowed, labelled)
category purchase rate per buyer if known
customer-level purchases for at least 12 months (ideally 24)
Unique buyers per quarter and new buyers per quarter (POS, Shopify, Stripe, bookings)
Purchases or orders per buyer per quarter
Buyer-level purchase counts for a frequency distribution
Capacity utilisation (bookable slots used) for service businesses
Size of the reachable market where it is listable (B2B niche)
missing_data_behavior: No active count: no ceiling; show the formula only.
Churn typed by the owner: show source and a wide range.

decision_branches.if: Churn high for the business's size and controllable
Churn normal for size, growth goal needs more buyers
decision_branches.then: Penetration first; keep acquisition at least at replacement.
Double-jeopardy flag: growth usually comes mostly from more buyers.

implementation_steps: Compute steady-state ceiling = new customers per month / monthly churn (code)
Compute replacement acquisition = churn x current base
Compare churn to a reference only where one exists (SaaS) and note size effect
Allocate: fix controllable churn first only when it is above the norm; never zero acquisition
Decompose sales = buyers x purchases per buyer (code, not prose)
State the target in both terms
Check frequency against category rate and against peers if known
Compute revenue share of top 20%, middle 30%, bottom 50% (code)
Compare two consecutive periods for the same customers before calling anyone 'VIP'
Size the light/non-buyer pool in reach
Pull quarterly unique buyers, new buyers and purchases
Decompose growth into change in buyers and change in purchases per buyer (in code)
Compute the purchase-frequency distribution and the top-20% share of purchases (Pareto share)
dependencies: consistent definition of an active customer
a repeat-purchase category with several substitutes
enough customers for deciles (rule of thumb: 100+)
Transactions linked to a customer ID for at least two quarters
Capacity is not the binding constraint (diagnosis.ts delivery check)
metrics: share of churn that is controllable
share of new vs returning buyers
next-period share of last period's top 20%
share of sales from last period's non-buyers
Pareto share (top 20% of buyers' share of purchases)
guardrails: Top 20% of buyers give about half of volume, not 80%; heavy buyers regress.
No '5x cheaper to retain' or '5% retention = 100% profit' claims (no empirical basis per ch3)
Retention plays must say what share of churn they can touch
Never present a frequency-only plan as the default for a repeat-purchase consumer business without the double-jeopardy note
Don't build segments or lookalikes on a single period's heavy buyers without the moderation caveat
Don't present a loyalty program as the growth engine without a penetration mechanism
Label Ehrenberg-Bass patterns as consumer/repeat defaults, not laws for every business
Arithmetic done in code, never estimated in prose
alternatives_when_constrained: No churn reasons: run 5-10 exit interviews or a one-question cancel survey first
No churn rate: use repeat-rate proxy; mark retention 'unknown' (as diagnosis.ts:99 does for non-SaaS)
No buyer-level data: use transactions and a customer-count estimate, labelled; or run a 4-week receipt or booking-name tally
No category size: skip penetration %, keep buyer counts
No customer IDs: skip; use category-buyer reach logic
No customer IDs: use new versus returning customer counts from the last 90 days
No transaction data: add a measurement first step and keep plays cheap and reversible (diagnosis 'unknown' path)
stop_conditions: If a retention fix runs one renewal cycle and churn is unchanged, return effort to acquisition
Review after one full purchase cycle; if buyers grew but frequency did not, that is the expected pattern, not failure
If a heavy-buyer program shows member lift, check against the moderation baseline before expanding
Review quarterly. If two quarters show growth mainly from purchases per buyer while buyers are flat, and the business is niche- or capacity-limited, keep the loyalty-led plan and record it.
review_triggers: Owner's numbers or business type change
A dated benchmark this playbook mentions is superseded
SaaS with high voluntary early churn: Sharp's low-defection examples do not apply
Very small bases: churn rates noisy month to month
Contracted B2B or SaaS where 'frequency' is seat or usage expansion
Short analysis windows exaggerate or understate concentration
Single-provider subscriptions (dentist, accountant) where repertoires are tiny

contextual_heuristic.rule: proposed rule: diagnosis output adds a computed steady-state ceiling (newCustomersPerMonth / monthlyChurn) and replacement acquisition (monthlyChurn x active customers) whenever both inputs exist
proposed rule: COMPETING.retention also names 'defection outside the business's control (moved, closed, no longer needs) and normal size-related churn'
proposed rule: when retention binds, the plan still keeps acquisition at or above replacement level unless capacity binds

proposed rule: when a plan's goal implies purchases-per-buyer growth above 20% with flat buyers in a repeat-purchase B2C business, the plan must also show the penetration-led version and label the frequency version as against the norm
proposed rule: retention or VIP plays aimed at last period's heaviest buyers carry a note that next period they will buy less on average without any change (buyer moderation)
proposed: When top customers are identified from one period, state that about half may not be top customers next period, and don't size a VIP program from a single period.

proposed: When the diagnosis is retention for a consumer repeat business, add the competing explanation that higher defection is normal for a small brand and often circumstantial; require a churn-reason split before product changes.

strategic_preference.rule: proposed rule: block copy or plans that cite 'retention is 5x cheaper' or 'a 5% retention gain doubles profit' as fact
proposed rule: for B2C repeat-purchase businesses, at least one acquisition play reaches light or non-buyers of the brand

proposed: For consumer repeat-purchase types that aren't capacity-bound, the bankable demand play must recruit new or light category buyers; a loyalty, VIP or referral play can't be labelled the growth engine unless a capacity or listable-niche condition is recorded.

missing_prerequisite.rule: proposed rule: before labelling churn weak for a non-SaaS business, collect churn reasons
proposed rule: if buyer-level counts are missing, ask for them before setting a frequency target
proposed rule: any 'top customers' statistic must come from data with the period stated; never assume 80/20
proposed: Growth decomposition, Pareto share and heavy-buyer stability are computed by deterministic calculators from owner data.

economic_feasibility.rule: proposed rule: required purchases per buyer greater than the category purchase rate is infeasible and must be blocked by a deterministic check
